Objective for processing:  
The University of Oxford’s Big Health Data Group (BHDG) requests an extract of PROMs data and linked HES data related to patients who had hip and/or knee surgery since 2009.  The data is to be used in a NIHR-funded Health Technology Assessment (HTA) project: ‘Introducing Standardized and Evidence Based Thresholds for Hip and Knee Replacement Surgery. The Arthroplasty Candidacy Help Engine (The ACHE tool)’. 
The study will identify scoring systems and clinical and economic thresholds that can be used to select candidates for hip and knee surgery.
The main output of the project will be the development of a clinical tool (the ACHE tool) that clinicians can use to identify which patients with hip or knee pain should be referred to secondary care and help inform patients’ and clinicians’ decisions about hip and knee surgery. The ACHE tool will be based on a scoring system (questionnaire) and a set of evidence based thresholds.

Processing activities: 
Two departments within the University of Oxford will collaborate on the project.  The data will be supplied to the Big Health Data Group (BHDG) at the Nuffield Department of Orthopaedic, Rheumatology & Musculoskeletal Science (NDORMS) who will share a copy of the data with the Health Economics Research Centre (HERC) at the Nuffield Department of Population Health.
Statisticians at the BHDG will analyse the data to establish general hip/knee severity threshold levels for the Oxford Knee Scores (OKS) and the Oxford Hip Scores (OHS) using multilevel modelling.  These thresholds will be used to estimate candidacy for hip/knee surgeries.  The analysis will not only focus on pre-operative and post-operative Oxford Knee Scores and Oxford Hip Scores, but also on relevant pre-operative co-variables including age, obesity, co-morbidities, radiographic changes, smoking/alcohol use and psychological factors derived from the HES and the PROMS data.
Economists at the HERC will assess the cost-effectiveness of patients with different baseline Oxford Knee Scores (OKS) and Oxford Hip Scores; estimate economic thresholds above which joint replacement is not cost-effective, and evaluate the cost-effectiveness of using the ACHE tool to select patients for joint replacement. 
The data will not be linked with any other datasets and will not be shared with any third party beyond the collaborating departments at University of Oxford.  The data will be used exclusively for the purpose of the ACHE project, until the end of the project.  It is possible that the University of Oxford will apply to amend these conditions to allow the linkage of HES/PROMS data with National Joint Registry data but no linkage will take place without the explicit permission of the HSCIC.
At the end of the study, the data will be safely held in a password protected University Computer at the Botnar Research Centre, for further 5 years, and accessed only to answer questions arising from the publication and other publicity.

Specific outputs expected, including target date: 
The outputs of this analysis will comprise publications submitted to open-access peer reviewed journals and an HTA monograph.  The statistics and health economics work is due to be completed in 2015 and submitted for journal publication in 2016 or in early 2017.
The monograph describing the study as a whole will be published in Health Technology Assessment and is expected to be published in June 2017. All outputs will present only aggregated data (e.g. sample means, regression coefficients and estimated thresholds) with small numbers suppressed.
The University of Oxford currently plans to submit at least one paper on the study to The British Medical Journal (BMJ) and submit papers to other peer reviewed journals, such as BMJ Open; Bone and Joint Research; Medical Decision-Making; Health Economics, and Value in Health. 
Besides publications in leading peer review journals, the results of the study will be presented to the Patient and Research Engagement Forum (PREF) at the Nuffield Orthopedics Centre (NOC). The purpose of PREF is to involve, inform and educate patients & public about research in Oxford, improving its relevance, quality and appropriateness from the patient’s perspective. 
Furthermore, the NOC Network will run a ‘Joint Venture’ event, which is an interactive public information event focusing on our research, culminating with a discussion and Q&A session.
In addition to publications, this project will produce a clinical tool (the ACHE tool) to be used by GPs, orthopaedic surgeons and/or other health professionals to select patients for referral and/or knee and hip replacement.  The tool will not contain any of the record level data used for the creation of scoring systems and clinical and economic thresholds. 
The University of Oxford anticipates that the Arthroplasty Candidacy Help Engine (ACHE) clinical tool will first be piloted in the NHS in 2016 and available for use in the NHS from 2017.  It is anticipated that the tool will be used across the NHS, freely available to all GPs and referral hubs. In addition the tool will be used in secondary care as a reference point for clinical consultation. The tool will be delivered via a web-based platform that is already in development. It is anticipated that the tool would be a multivariable predictive model, based on an established clinical score that is easy to understand and use. 
The National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) specifically requested research to develop tools for NHS health professionals to use to select patients for joint replacement as part of a call for research projects.  The University of Oxford’s clinical tool will not be a project to be marketed and sold.
No other third party application or intellectual property included in the final output/product will result in this data being used for sales and marketing purposes.

Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care including target date: 
The project as a whole will produce the ACHE tool for assessing patients with hip arthritis, knee arthritis or those with arthritis of both hips and knees that can be used in primary care to identify candidates for hip and knee joint replacement, guiding referral to secondary care. Incorporating the tool into the NHS patient pathway is intended to standardise patient care, reduce unwarranted variation and improve patient outcome. The ACHE tool aims to establish best practice criteria for which patients should be referred for joint replacement that are based on scientific evidence. This is intended to ensure that everyone gets fair access to joint replacement based on the severity of their symptoms, rather than where they live. At present, average preoperative scores vary between different regions of the country. 
It is envisaged that introducing evidence-based criteria for which patients are referred for joint replacement will improve patient outcomes (by ensuring that everyone who can benefit is referred) and reduce unnecessary costs (by avoiding referral of patients who are unlikely to benefit from surgery).  The project is due to be completed by December 2016.    Use of the ACHE tool will be included in the NHS Commissioning Guidance for hip & knee surgery, ensuring uptake into NHS practice. The University of Oxford anticipate that the ACHE tool could be used by the NHS from 2017.
